lesson.title: Before You Trust the Interval: Checking the Conditions
lesson.summary: The one-proportion z-interval is only valid when three conditions, Random, 10 percent, and Large Counts, are satisfied, because those conditions are what make the normal approximation behind the formula reasonable.
lesson.body:
The formula p-hat plus or minus z star times the standard error looks like it works for any sample proportion you plug into it, but the formula secretly depends on an assumption: that the sampling distribution of p-hat is approximately normal, centered at the true p, with standard deviation sqrt(p(1-p)/n). That assumption is exactly what the earlier idea of conditions for the standard deviation of a proportion is about, and it does not hold automatically. Before trusting a computed interval, you have to check three conditions.

The Random condition requires that the data come from a random sample or a randomized experiment. Without randomness, there is no statistical basis for generalizing the sample proportion to the population at all, no formula can repair a biased sampling method. The 10 percent condition applies when sampling without replacement from a finite population, it requires the sample size n to be no more than about 10 percent of the population size, so that individual observations are close enough to independent for the standard error formula to be accurate. The Large Counts condition, sometimes called the success-failure condition, requires n times p-hat to be at least 10 and n times (1 minus p-hat) to be at least 10. This is the condition that specifically justifies using a normal curve, and therefore a z star value, rather than some skewed distribution, because with too few expected successes or failures the sampling distribution of p-hat is lopsided rather than bell-shaped.

Return to the voter survey from the previous chapter: 400 voters sampled, with p-hat = 0.55. Checking Large Counts, n times p-hat = 400 times 0.55 = 220, and n times (1 minus p-hat) = 400 times 0.45 = 180. Both are comfortably above 10, so the normal approximation is reasonable and the z-interval computed earlier, 0.501 to 0.599, can be trusted, provided the survey was also conducted randomly and 400 voters is no more than 10 percent of all registered voters in the relevant population (true for any realistic city, state, or national election).

Conditions matter most when they fail. Imagine surveying only 15 people and finding 2 successes, then n times p-hat is only 2, far below 10. The sampling distribution of p-hat in that case is noticeably skewed, and a z-interval built on it can have much worse than the advertised coverage rate, meaning the interval is less likely than claimed to actually capture the true proportion. Checking conditions is not a formality tacked onto the end of a calculation, it is the difference between an interval that means what it claims and one that does not.
